articles.title: Meta Internal Muse AI Triggers Employee Surveillance Uproar
articles.content: Meta employees have raised concerns about the company’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters . Recommended Video In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal. “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted. A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported. Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.” Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.” In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters. “These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.” The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations. A Meta spokesperson said employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback in order to implement privacy safeguards, adding that employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public does and that some functions aren’t available elsewhere. As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android users have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse. “With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained. Since Muse was launched in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social-media giant’s plan to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI. But other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf. Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents. The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages . In recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo , United Airlines , Apple , and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out. Because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times . In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino , Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages. “This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. The show transforms Fortune ’s trusted reporting into actionable, conversational, and entertaining insights for an emerging class of business leaders. Watch here.

articles.title: Civil Liberties Coalitions Battle Backdoor Mass Surveillance Reauthorization Maneuver
articles.content: In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization . Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill. The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.” You can read the entire letter here . Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. Once it does, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and several other agencies give themselves permission to search through U.S. persons’ data without a warrant. This is unconstitutional, undermines our right to private communications, and creates a dangerous and potent tool for would-be despots who might use that communication to discriminate, marginalize, or punish people based on their identities and political beliefs. This is not the kind of policy Congress should be considering without necessary reforms, open debate, and the ability for lawmakers to vote against without forcing them to vote “no” on all defense policy. We once again urge Congress not to put Section 702’s future in a must-pass bill like the NDAA.

articles.title: Cascading Power Grid Disruptions Threaten Unprepared Cloud Infrastructure
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here . week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks , United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame. So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs . Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up. Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates . Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.” External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences. “Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.” “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.” Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts. Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000 . To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025. In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI. There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.” , at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year. “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.” Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg. In Other News • Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters . The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors. • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “ wrench attacks ”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage . • Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports , the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order. Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected] . And stay safe out there.

articles.title: Google Erases Classic Search Button in Radical AI Transformation
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely. Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone. The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search. The new AI-centric search homepage The new AI-centric search homepage The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.” It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results. The current (old) Google search homepage. Credit: Google The current (old) Google search homepage. Credit: Google This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction. articles.title: Engineered Mosquito Trials Drastically Suppress Dengue Transmission Rates
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Adult Aedes mosquitoes on display in Singapore to mark 10 years of Project Wolbachia, an initiative to control dengue through the release of lab-grown mosquitoes. ST PHOTO: LIM YAOHUI Published Nov 22, 2026, 12:16 AM Updated Nov 22, 2026, 10:11 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Scientists found that Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes cut dengue and chikungunya infections in Brazilian children by about 69%, even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak. The four-year study in Belo Horizonte tested blood from more than 5,700 children and compared neighbourhoods with and without released Wolbachia mosquitoes. Experts said the method could work with pesticides and other controls to reduce dengue further, as Florida faces a large local outbreak and the strategy spreads worldwide. AI generated WASHINGTON – Children who lived in Brazilian neighbourhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported on Nov 21. The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. In neighbourhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighbourhoods – an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr Sri Edupuganti, of Emory University, part of the international research team. The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any US state since at least the 1940s. Usually in the continental US, dengue is found mostly in people who travelled internationally. But as of Nov 20, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Outside the US, the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects – males and females – into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighbourhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease. AP Dengue fever Chikungunya Mosquito Brazil Science

articles.title: Deep Space Interceptor Validates Autonomous Planetary Kinetic Defense Architecture
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story the subject of Hollywood movies , but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “ Tunguska Event ,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion. Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites . It will even be visible to the naked eye. In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions . As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technolog y that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time. In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit . Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth. Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body , measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos. The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA launched the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos. by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet —the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it. But questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars , the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November. Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration , and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability. But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation. and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface . Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel. The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites . Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface . Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks . According to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space . In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000. articles.title: Colombian Healthtech Startups Build Fintech Rails Around Collapsing Insurers
articles.content: Colombia's Entidades Promotoras de Salud (EPSs), the companies that manage public health funds and pay hospitals and clinics on behalf of the country's insured population, closed 2025 with $58.06 trillion Colombian pesos ($16 billion USD) in obligations, according to the Comptroller General's Office. The hospitals and clinics that provide care, known as IPSs, absorb much of that pressure. As of June this year, the 232 that report to the Colombian Association of Hospitals and Clinics were owed 27.8 trillion pesos, with 60.5% of it overdue.  That makes Colombia a hard place to sell healthtech. In much of the country, the EPSs are the main buyer for the kind of care these companies provide.  Three Colombian founders are building anyway. Ximena Ruget of Glya, María Artunduaga of Samay, and Valentina Agudelo of Salva Health are among the 15 winners of the 2026 Bayer Foundation Women Entrepreneurs Award, selected from 1,172 applications across 124 countries.  Each will receive €25,000 in non-dilutive funding and six months of acceleration with the Impact Hub network.  "The EPSs are in a very complicated situation right now," Agudelo said. "Saying they have money problems is putting it mildly."  The problem extends across the region, too. The Pan American Health Organization estimates that noncommunicable diseases and mental health conditions will cost South America more than $7.3 trillion USD between 2020 and 2050. Meanwhile, Latin American healthtech drew just $253.3 million in investment in 2024.  "The more important thing is understanding the payment and who gives me my reimbursement code," Artunduaga told Contxto. "You start from the end and work backwards."  Artunduaga's company makes Sylvee, a chest patch that sends sound into the lungs and reads how they resonate with the goal of detecting chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and its flare-ups without a hospital visit.  Medical devices usually spend years in regulatory review before they earn anything. Samay found revenue sooner by developing AI algorithms for pharmaceutical companies and device makers.  In Medellín, the company runs clinical trials in which respiratory therapists take a hospital lung function machine into patients' homes, so Sylvee can be trained to match its readings. The founder said a clinical research organization told her it would offer Sylvee to its pharma clients if the algorithm works. Those trials can pay up to $350 per patient per month.  "I no longer need to go to the FDA to try to sell the device right away," she stressed.  Pharma has its own reason to pay: a patient diagnosed three to five years earlier is a patient who gets treatment sooner and is better managed. "Pharma is a strategic ally for me," Artunduaga stressed. "It benefits all of us." The EPSs remain the long term buyer, and Samay has opened talks with Invima, Colombia's health regulator, and expects to launch Sylvee in Colombia in early 2028. Until then, the company is building the evidence it will need to show insurers the savings.  "Clinical evidence is everything," she said. "When you prove something, people don't fight it."  Agudelo's company makes Julieta, a portable device that flags breast cancer risk in under 10 minutes, without internet, a power outlet or a specialist required.  Its biggest buyer is local government. "We approach the mayor's office first, and from there the health secretariat, which is who actually funds the projects. The funding goes to the public hospital, and the public hospital is the one that hires us," Agudelo explained to Contxto.  The model works because women already trust their local hospital. In Maicao, a city in Colombia's northern department of La Guajira, Salva and the town's public hospital tested 3,000 women in 30 days. Julieta flagged 42 as high-risk, and all of them got a mammogram.  "The health system no longer has to worry about 3,000 women, but about 42," Agudelo said.  Salva doesn't stop at the test, though. An in-house tracking team calls every flagged woman, and when an EPS stalls on follow-up care, the team calls the mayor, the health secretary, or the insurer.  The company has three more revenue lines: corporate screening days paid for by employers such as Google, Cine Colombia and Crepes & Waffles, devices loaned to clinics, and a home service. Salva has raised about $2.5 million, led most recently by Colombian fund Ewa Capital, and already operates in Guatemala, with Venezuela next.  "It will always be cheaper to have a woman who never had to go through chemotherapy because we caught it in time," Agudelo said of the cost benefit of Julieta for EPSs and the wider health system. Glya monitors chronic patients at home. Its own device sends readings from glucometers and blood pressure cuffs, and patients can also send photos of their readings on WhatsApp to Glady, the company's AI assistant.  The platform has flagged more than 56,000 health alerts across 1,400 patients, according to the Bayer award press release.  Glya sells to institutions. Its private customers are insurers and healthcare providers, and its public market is primary care centers in Colombia's regions.  "Something that's common to all three of us co-founders is selling," Ruget said.  Public institutions are slow to sign until they see results, so Glya has to fund pilots before any revenue comes in. The Bayer money will help cover that gap.  "This kind of grant lets us run those free trials and cover them financially until the agreements start billing," the co-founder, now working as Glya's board president and chief growth officer, explained.  Its strongest proof point comes from Hospital Universitario San Ignacio in Bogotá, where a hospital-at-home monitoring pilot became a permanent service. Glya has supported more than 1,000 chemotherapy sessions given at home, with only two of the 136 cancer patients it monitored having had adverse events.  "The patient feels more supported, feels they're in their own environment, that they don't have to travel," Ruget said.  For women founders in Latin America, capital is scarce. Female-only founding teams received 2.3% of global venture capital in 2024, and healthtech, which needs long clinical timelines and regulatory approval before it earns, is among the hardest sectors to fund.  But Agudelo emphasized this is part of why awards like Bayer's carry weight beyond their size. The program targets founders in low and middle-income countries, and this year's 15 winners came from across Latin America, Africa, and Asia.  "Objectively, we've seen much more return in the connections, the impact and the strength of having Bayer as an ally than in what we can do with the 25,000," she said. Meeting the other winners in Amsterdam in October also changed how she sees the market. The problems Salva tackles in La Guajira look much the same across the Global South, only at far larger scale.  "Everything we see in Colombia is 50 times smaller than what you see in Bangladesh," Agudelo said. "It's the same problem, but a billion people have it."  "It opens commercial doors, brings investors closer and even makes us think a little bigger," she said. articles.title: Congressional Leaders Demand Whistleblower Protections for Prediction Market Insider Trading
articles.content: Casten, Lieu propose whistleblower program for prediction market insider trading by Ford McCracken - 11/20/26 6:58 PM ET Link copied - 11/20/26 6:58 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Reps. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) and Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) introduced new legislation Friday to regulate prediction markets and prevent insider trading, allowing whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing. The Policing Insider Trading in Prediction Markets Act would create a program at the Justice Department for people with knowledge of insider trading to come forward and potentially receive financial compensation for information leading to successful enforcement. “Prediction markets have a serious insider trading problem,” Casten said. “By encouraging whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing, we can take an important step in cracking down on insider trading to restore accountability and public confidence in the U.S. rule of law.” Improper use of betting markets has been in the spotlight multiple times this year, among political candidates, service members and even White House staff. In August, President Trump’s teleprompter operator was placed on leave and investigated for placing bets on the content of the president’s speeches before they were made public. Later that month, a Republican congressional candidate in North Carolina was suspended from Kalshi for betting on her own race. Kalshi had previously suspended three other congressional candidates in April. Other examples of misuse include a U.S. Army soldier betting on the U.S. operation in Venezuela and nine accounts on Polymarket making $2.4 million on bets about military action in Iran. House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) announced an investigation into Kalshi and Polymarket in May. In a statement about the bill Friday, Lieu cited some of the examples as a reason for legislative action. “Government insiders should not be able to profit from betting on U.S. military operations or the contents of a President’s speech. They should not be able to use their positions of public trust to manipulate prediction markets,” Lieu said. Kalshi recently said it had eliminated the option to place bets on Trump’s comments in response to a Commodity Futures Trading Commission order, having previously argued that Trump-mention markets “present a heightened risk of manipulation.” With Republicans still in the majority, Casten and Lieu’s bill will need bipartisan support to pass before the end of the year, though it could be reintroduced once the new Congress — with a sizable Democratic majority — is sworn in. articles.title: Epoch AI Recomputes Foundational Compute Trends Behind Trillion-Dollar Capex
articles.content: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down. Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task. In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming. It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.” Artificial intelligence Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. articles.title: Wikipedia Editorial Capture Degrades Frontier Large Language Model Truth
articles.content: Danielle Shapiro Wikipedia’s War on Neutrality A new history of the online encyclopedia ignores its well-documented progressive bias. / Arts and Culture , Technology and Innovation November 20, 2026 Photo by Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images / Books & Culture / Arts and Culture , Technology and Innovation Nov 20 2026 The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia , by Richard Cooke (W.W. Norton & Company, 320 pp., $29.99) Since its early 2000s launch, Wikipedia has cultivated a reputation among educated professionals as a dependable, if quirky, source of information vetted by the wisdom of consensus and community editors. When biases arose over the years, skeptics were told that these were necessary growing pains of a massive, open-source project serving the common good. today. This assumption of benign neutrality rests on the idea that Wikipedia is simply a website by and for curious people seeking to democratize knowledge much like the printing press. Richard Cooke’s new history of the organization, The Last Best Place on the Internet , is the latest work to indulge this naivete. Cooke rightly identifies Wikipedia’s critical role in shaping the modern information ecosystem, but he refuses to acknowledge the platform as a captured institution that will train artificial intelligence to treat progressive orthodoxy as the only legitimate viewpoint. Wikipedia began in 2001 as an informal feeder project for Nupedia, an ambitious online encyclopedia founded the previous year by internet entrepreneur Jimmy Wales and philosopher Larry Sanger. Nupedia was conceived during the early dot-com boom to challenge the dominance in reference-text publishing of industry stalwarts such as Encyclopedia Britannica and Microsoft’s Encarta. Wales and Sanger believed that an unprecedented combination of open-content licensing, digital distribution, and an unpaid global labor pool could distinguish Nupedia and, in Cooke’s words, “remake the world.” Yet Nupedia’s editorial process, which included seven rigid steps of peer review, editing, and fact-checking, stalled the project almost immediately. Rather than inspiring a grassroots campaign to expand accessible knowledge, the cumbersome workflow alienated contributors. Wales conceded that his own drafting of an article felt more like “homework.” In the site’s first five months, only a single article, on the musical concept of “atonality,” reached publication quality, and the minimal web traffic suggested a bleak future for the great experiment. Moreover, the dot-com crash depleted any capital that Wales’s parent company could have used to salvage the site by paying moderators. Yet according to Cooke, it was Nupedia’s spectacular failure that allowed its founders to reimagine the project and conceive of the idea that eventually became Wikipedia. At a dinner in late 2000, computer programmer Ben Kovitz introduced Sanger to the “wiki” model (named after the Hawaiian word for “quick”), which eliminated traditional editorial gatekeeping by allowing anyone to draft or edit an article in real time. Realizing its capacity to bypass Nupedia’s bottlenecks, Sanger boldly emailed the project’s mailing list on January 10, 2001: “Let’s make a Wiki,” he proposed, encouraging skeptical academics to “humor me . . . Go there and add a little article. It will take all of five or ten minutes.” Thus was born Wikipedia. By the end of 2001, Wikipedia had published thousands of articles across 16 languages. The site’s real-time coverage of September 11 cemented its advantage over legacy reference sources as an agile, living archive that could document history as it unfolded. In 2003, amid threats of Spanish Wikipedia’s defection if the site elected to run advertisements, Wales solidified Wikipedia’s status as a nonprofit, launching the Wikimedia Foundation, which still governs the platform today. Yet Wikipedia’s anarchical structure almost imploded the project early on. Sanger left in March 2002 in protest over the lack of editorial discipline and refusal to police bad actors abusing the site. After several editorial scandals that threatened the platform’s credibility in the ensuing years, Wales, too, had to confront the possibility that an egalitarian ethos undermined the platform’s goal to be taken seriously. To impose order, Wales established editing restrictions and committees to govern the site. By 2007, power over editing was functionally consolidated into the hands of veteran insiders who could navigate Wikipedia’s arcane bylaws and devote extended time to curation. The site’s early “inclusionist” ethos, which celebrated entries on esoteric subjects and cultural minutiae, yielded to the “deletionists,” who sought to gatekeep the types of articles considered for publication. The most consequential of these new mandates was the codification of strict sourcing guidelines that empowered tenured editors to determine which publications counted as reliable. In time, this shift would effectively outsource Wikipedia’s standard of truth to a legacy-press apparatus increasingly dominated by progressive orthodoxy. Cooke views this bureaucratic maturation as a triumph. To the extent that he acknowledges bias on the platform, his concerns are merely demographic: he laments the site’s heavily male editor base, its Western-centric focus, and gender gaps in the platform’s profiles. Yet his authoring of a comprehensive history of Wikipedia in 2026 without mentioning its systemic blacklisting of conservative media or its purging of pro-Israel perspectives requires what amounts to an intellectual abdication. Beginning with its 2017 decision to deprecate the U.K.’s Daily Mail as a “generally unreliable” source whose reference use ought to be “generally prohibited,” Wikipedia editors abandoned the case-by-case evaluation of individual citations in favor of a centralized classification regime that would designate news outlets as “reliable” or “unreliable” and purge claims derived from those deemed unfit. Fox News’s political reporting, along with the New York Post and the Daily Wire , were all stamped as “ generally unreliable ” sources, while The Nation and the New York Times maintained general reliability status. In perhaps the most egregious example of this double standard, administrators prevented the New York Post ’s Hunter Biden disclosures from appearing as a recognized subject on the site only weeks before the 2020 election. These biases extend beyond the confines of domestic American politics. In June 2024, following a sustained campaign by anti-Zionist editors coordinating in private, off-site Discord servers, Wikipedia downgraded the Anti-Defamation League (ADL)—one of America’s oldest Jewish civil rights organizations—to “generally unreliable” on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the definition of anti-Semitism itself. While mainstream Jewish outlets and organizations like the ADL and Jewish Virtual Library were labeled as unreliable sources, Qatar’s state-sponsored Al Jazeera , which routinely broadcasts Hamas propaganda, remains “generally reliable.” Unsurprisingly, Wikipedia’s decisions have disseminated a distorted view of Jewish and Israeli history. Wikipedia’s page on Zionism once described the term as “the national movement of the Jewish people that supports the re-establishment of a Jewish homeland in the territory defined as the historic Land of Israel”; the definition today reads, “an ethnic nationalist movement that emerged in late 19th century Europe to establish and support a Jewish homeland through colonization in the region of Palestine.” Cooke is correct in his thesis that Wikipedia’s modern dominance stems from its role as the bedrock for AI, yet his book falls flat by ignoring how the platform’s biases have corrupted that very data. In a future where AI likely shapes the average American’s outlook and becomes a crucial tool in policing, education, and government, the possibility that the information underlying these important functions is corrupted should concern all Americans. While The Last Best Place on the Internet offers a fascinating history of Wikipedia and accurately assesses the encyclopedia’s current power, the book tells only half the story. In refusing to examine where Wikipedia has gone wrong, Cooke was either ignorant of the organization’s full history or complicit in its attempt to brand itself as the neutral public square. articles.title: European Lawmakers Challenge Legality of Outsourced Biometric Deportation Hubs
articles.content: Plans by five member states and Rwanda to establish a migrant return hub, as confirmed on Monday (16 November), could be in violation of EU human rights obligations – and liberal and leftwing MEPs are asking the European commission to review its legality. On Monday (23 November), at least 40 MEPs from the Greens/EFA, the Left, Socialists and Democrats, and liberal Renew, will write to the EU Commission to express concerns Rwanda may be unable to fulfil key conditions under Europe’s return regulation.  They are worried about international human rights standards being applied toward any people who might end up being hosted in Rwandan return hubs. In 2023, the UK’s Supreme Court blocked migrant transfers to the east African nation on the basis of human rights concerns and the principle of non-refoulement. Despite no agreement having yet being signed with Kigali, leaders and ministers from Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands announced in Vienna last Monday that a “partnership” had been agreed. Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, joined them in Austria to say human rights concerns were founded on “cliches.” The group met amid outstanding technical issues, with deportations to mainland Africa’s most densely populated country expected to start in 2027. Migrants from as far afield as Afghanistan could end up in Rwanda, a country most of them would have no connection to, if their asylum applications were rejected in the EU and they do not voluntarily comply with a return order.  Right-wing and far-right groups in the European Parliament rammed through the return regulation, which broadly mandates deportations, in June. A letter by 22 EU leaders in August also urged the acceleration of the process after the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in north Africa in July.  Inscribed as a political footnote, the caveat on human rights monitoring in the return regulation is still to be seen working in practice, but MEPs still aim to hold the commission to its obligations as guardian of European treaties, in which it monitors the implementation of EU laws. articles.title: Finnish Air Force Tests Highway Combat Dispersal Under Arctic Conditions
articles.content: Ilmavoimien vuoden pääsota­harjoitus on ensimmäinen testi Jännevirran uudelle varalaskupaikalle Siilinjärvellä Pohjois-Savossa. Varalaskupaikka valmistui viime vuoden lopulla , ja se sijaitsee valtatiellä 9 Karjalan lennoston tukikohdan tuntumassa. Valtatie 9 Kuopion ja Joensuun välillä on ollut poikki liikenteeltä Jännevirralla keskiviikosta alkaen. Tänään varalaskupaikalla on vilkasta lentotoimintaa, ja Protective Fence 2026 -harjoitusta esiteltiin aamupäivällä medialle. Karjalan lennoston hävittäjälentolaivue 31:n komentaja, everstiluutnantti Tomi Lyytinen kertoo videolla, että Hornetilla laskeutuminen varalaskupaikalle jännittää kokenuttakin lentäjää: Video: Toni Pitkänen / Yle, Sami Takkinen / Yle Suomalaisten Hornet-hävittäjien lisäksi Jännevirran varalaskupaikkaa käyttää harjoituksessa muun muassa kahdeksan F-35-hävittäjää Alankomaiden kuninkaallisista ilma- ja avaruusvoimista. Mediatilaisuudessa oli tarkoitus nähdä alankomaalaishävittäjien laskeutuminen, mutta huono sää esti suunnitelmat. Joukko harjoittelee nyt ensimmäistä kertaa nousuja ja laskuja maantietukikohdasta. Karjalan lennoston komentajan, eversti Tomi Böhmin mukaan alankomaalaisilla on omat turvallisuusmääräyksensä. – Koska tämä on ensimmäinen kerta, ei ole mielekästä nostaa riskitasoa liian korkeaksi. Alankomaiden kuninkaallisten ilma- ja avaruusvoimien 322. hävittäjälentolaivueen komentaja, everstiluutnantti Pascal Smaal kertoo, että heidän lentäjänsä eivät ole tottuneita maantietukikohtiin tai lumisiin olosuhteisiin. – Laskeutuminen ei sinänsä ole vaikeaa, koska tie on niin leveä. Tien pinnan jäätyminen sen sijaan on haaste. Avaa kuvien katselu Pascal Smaal laivueineen harjoittelee nyt ensimmästä kertaa maantietukikohdassa toimimista. Kuva: Toni Pitkänen / Yle Tomi Böhmin mukaan harjoituksen kannalta huono sää on osittain jopa tervetullutta. – Yksi vuorokausi saisi olla erittäin huonoa säätä, jotta pääsemme testaamaan, toimiiko laskupaikan huolto riittävän hyvin. Suomen ensimmäiset omat F-35-hävittäjät saapuivat Rovaniemelle syyskuussa , mutta ne eivät osallistu harjoitukseen. Tomi Böhm kertoo videolla, että Suomen omien F-35-hävittäjien vastaanottotarkastus on vielä kesken: Video: Toni Pitkänen / Yle, Sami Takkinen / Yle Harjoituksessa nähdään myös Ranskan ilma- ja avaruusvoimien Rafale-hävittäjiä. Ne operoivat Rovaniemeltä. Lisäksi Ruotsin ilmavoimien JAS 39 Gripen -hävittäjät lentävät omasta kotitukikohdastaan Kallaxista. Harjoituksessa on mukana myös suomalainen avaruusteknologiayhtiö Iceye, joka on Ilmavoimien yhteistyökumppani. Se valmistaa pieniä tutkasatelliitteja. Iceyen satelliittikuvat näyttävät joukoille, miten niiden toiminta näkyy avaruudesta. Komentaja Böhm kertoo, että se auttaa joukkoja oppimaan ja tarvittaessa korjaamaan taistelutapaansa. – Varusmiehet ja reserviläiset näkevät, miltä heidän toimintansa näyttää avaruudesta. Protective Fence -harjoituksessa Ilmavoimat saa yhtiön datasta palautteen kerran päivässä. Avaa kuvien katselu Iceye-yhtiön johtaja Seppo Aaltonen (vasemmalla) seurasi Ilmavoimien harjoitusta Jännevirran varalaskupaikalla. Kuva: Toni Pitkänen / Yle Runsaan viikon kestävään harjoitukseen osallistuu yli 40 lentokonetta ja noin 4 100 sotilasta. Heistä noin 1 800 on kertausharjoituksiin osallistuvia reserviläisiä.
